other vehicles" Is the advice of Earle
Brown, chief of the Minnesota High
way patrol. 1t is an act of courtesy to
other motorists, and also gives the driver
better light on the road Immediately
ahead of him, so it promotes safety all
around


Use of the depressed beam when
meeting other vehicles is not required
by law, Mr. Brown explains, as the
two filament lamps did not come into
general use until after the passage of
the uniform traffic act in 1927. Nor is
the use of the old style DINNERS" re-
quired in Minnesota. Use of DINNERS
is not recommended, because they do
not give enough light for safe driving.


The traffic act provides that all head
lamps must give sufficient light to make
a person observable 200 feet ahead,
under normal atmospheric conditions,
but no driving lamp shall project a
light glaring or dazzling to persons
ahead Lamps shall be deemed to COM
ply with the law if no part of the main
bright portion of the light beam rises
above plane passing through the
lamp centers parallel to the level road,
and in no case higher than AZ inches
rs feet ahead of the vehicle.


The upper beam on two-filament
lights must comply with this require
ment, and using the depressed beam
when meeting other vehicles will not
compensate for the use of an illegal
upper beam at other times. If the
upper beam does not comply with the
law, the lamps should be focused by
a trained lamp adjuster at an official
lamp adjusting station.


But even if the upper beam complies
with the law, safety and comfort will
be promoted by using the depressed
beam when meeting other drivers, Mr.
Brown said. In city driving or in
heavy traffic, he adds, it is good rule
to drop the lights and leave them
down.


With less traffic and more hours Of
darkness, the highway patrol during
the fall and winter will devote more
time to the war on glazing lights, lights
out of order, and any other failure
to comply with the lighting requirements
of the traffic act.

OKLAHOMA CITY. October a.
Gov. W. H. Murray announced yesterday legislative program including curtailment of wheat and cotton acreage and proposals for drastic tax reduction which he said he would submit to popular vote by initiative petition this Fall.

Free textbooks, limitation of time for corporation land holdings, and unemployment relief also are included in the program.

Perhaps the most far-reaching of the proposals is a projected constitutional amendment to abolish all ad valorem taxes for State purposes and to limit such taxes for city and county purposes to 15 mills. The present limit, including extra levies for schools is 49 mills.

"To Ring the Firebells."
Since the Legislature last Winter, when some of his reforms fell on deaf ears, the picturesque Governor has promised to ring the "firebells" in Oklahoma cities and hamlets and rally the people to his support.

The Governor indicated he would announce the election date as soon as he solves the problem of raising needed funds. Observers thought it would be early November.

Cotton planting would be curtailed for the next two years, as was authorized recently in Texas—through law preventing planting of more than 80 per cent of total cultivated acreage. A commission would be created with power to determine wheat acreage, and after 1888, cotton acreage.

There would be a $4,000,000 appropriation for free textbooks and the State might print them if they can't be bought satisfactorily.

One cent of a cent per gallon gasoline tax would relieve the jobless.

Corporations holding land more than 10 years would escheat to the State. This, said Murray, vitalizes constitutional provisions.

There may be another bill, the Governor said, if he can get around certain constitutional provisions of the Federal Constitution.

control prices or stife competition may
sooner or later expect antitrust charges
to be filed against it and its members,

Justice Is not in the slightest degree
hostile to what it considers the proper
activities and healthy growth of trade
associations. Cooperation Is not OPP

price-fixing.

practice adopted during the past five
years, at the commissions solicitation,
by so industries at trade-practice con-
ferences. These business codes were
approved by the commission at the
time of their adoption. Later the De-
partment of Justice found several IN
dustrieS engaged, pursuant to these
codes. in practices which it thought
contrary to the antitrust laws. Now
the commission. by its review, has with
drawn approval of those rules which 1t

fled against the sugar institute Is the
elimination of Investigations by both
the Trade Commission and the Depart
ment of Justice, these agencies ord1nar-

other. This policy, in fact, has led to
cross purposes. Neither requests the
other to institute proceedings under the
antitrust statutes. They cooperate
merely in the gathering of information
by investigations to avoid duplication
of work. Thus the information gathered
in the investigation which the commits
sion has made in reviewing the trade
practice codes will undoubtedly be
available to the Justice Department.
But no concerted or cooperative action
is anticipated.


Object of Laws.

seeking to enforce the antitrust
statutes at this particular time. APP
parently does not, in their opinion tend
to retard general business recovery. The
antitrust laws, it is pointed out, are
primarily aimed to protect economic OPP

of the thing is obvious, to note that
every member of the police establishment who chooses at this time to comment

practice of the third degree. The crime

partment long enough to wear the nap

one form or another, as long as there

third degree. One does not have to go
far to find the advocates. A good many

KANSAS CITY, October 8 (AP).—
Admiral Robert E. Coontz, U. S. N. retired, has asked Congress to stand by the Navy and support the Navy League in its differences with President Hoover growing out of the organization's position to Naval economies.

The league has charged the President with "abysmal ignorance of why Navies are maintained and of how they are used to accomplish their major mission." Mr. Hoover asserted the organization has disseminated "untruths and distortions of fact."
